After announcing modifications to the European version of App Tracking Transparency, Apple recently unveiled a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in Europe. Details below.

Apple modifies EU developer business terms

Apple had previously announced eight modifications to the European version of App Tracking Transparency, following an investigation by German antitrust regulators into the feature.

The company has now announced that a new commission structure will take effect in Europe on October 1, including lowering the link-out commission to 15% and replacing the controversial Core Technology Fee with a 5% "core technology commission".

These revisions come just over a year after Apple announced major changes to the EU App Store, which introduced a complex set of rules—details can be found here.

Below is Apple's official statement:

Apple is also announcing new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative payment options, and distributing apps via alternative app marketplaces or the web.

The new terms are as follows:

Apps distributed on the App Store using Apple's In-App Purchase system will be subject to a 26% commission; the vast majority of developers, including those in the App Store Small Business Programme, Mini Apps Partner Programme, or Video Partner Programme, as well as auto-renewing subscriptions after the first year, will pay 15%. Apps on the App Store using alternative payment processing will pay a 20% commission, with developers in the aforementioned programmes eligible for a reduced rate of 10%. App Store apps that link from within the app to an external website to complete a transaction will pay 15%, with developers in the aforementioned programmes eligible for a reduced rate of 10%. Apps distributed via alternative app marketplaces or the web will be subject to a 5% core technology commission from Apple.

Under the new terms, developers may also offer both Apple's In-App Purchase and alternative payment options, whether within the app or via a link to a website, provided they meet Apple's "display requirements" and maintain their chosen payment option for 12 months.

Today's announcement also includes a new round of child safety protections in the EU, as well as new rules for alternative payment options:

Apps in the App Store's "Kids" category will no longer contain links to external websites to complete transactions, reducing the risk of children falling victim to scams or deception. For users under 18, all App Store apps that use alternative payment processing or link to external websites for transactions must include a parental gate, requiring parental or guardian involvement before any purchase by a minor. For users under 13, App Store apps will not be permitted to link to external websites for transactions, protecting young children from scam risks.

Apple added that in EU member states where parental consent is required for digital activities involving children over 13, the relevant protections will be adjusted accordingly.

Finally, the changes announced by Apple today also expand eligibility for operating alternative app marketplaces or distributing apps via the web.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Achieving a moderate level of financial stability as rated by Dun & Bradstreet. Being a publicly listed company or owned by one. Having received venture capital financing from a sizable investment firm. Having completed a financial audit conducted by a licensed accounting firm. Being a government agency, educational institution, or non-profit organisation.

Apple noted that the web distribution option, currently available only in the EU, lacks ongoing oversight by a marketplace operator, meaning bad actors could potentially "operate undetected for extended periods, harming users".

Accordingly, Apple said it will continue to require all apps distributed through alternative channels to undergo its Notarization process.

To learn more about today's announcement, please visit this link.

Update: A European Commission spokesperson, in a statement to Bloomberg, said the Commission welcomes Apple's changes and noted that they are the result of "close dialogue" between the two parties. The spokesperson added that the Commission will closely monitor Apple's implementation of the new terms.

What are your thoughts on Apple's new rules for the EU? Let us know in the comments.
